papers.title: Shared human-machine control of an intelligent bionic hand improves grasping and decreases cognitive burden for transradial amputees
papers.notes: A sensor-equipped prosthetic hand shares control between a user’s EMG signals and a machine controller that helps position the fingers. Tests including four people with transradial amputations found improved grip precision and security and reduced cognitive burden.

details.abstract: Problem: multi-finger myoelectric control can be difficult and cognitively demanding. Proposal: continuously blend a user’s EMG-based commands with a sensor-driven controller that brings each finger toward an object while preserving user control of the grasp.
details.architecture: A single-hidden-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) predicts finger-to-object kinematic distance from fingertip proximity and pressure. A modified Kalman filter estimates the user’s intended five-digit position from surface EMG; a nonlinear rule blends the two control signals.
details.training: MLP training data came from moving individual digits toward and away from 3D-printed objects; contact positions supplied distance targets. For the Kalman decoder, participants attempted each digit’s flexion and extension along with the prosthesis: four trials per direction per digit. Of 528 EMG features, 48 were selected.
details.loss: The main paper does not specify the MLP training loss or optimization hyperparameters; see the referenced supplementary materials for further detail.
details.metrics: In a fragile-object transfer experiment with six participants without limb loss, success was 89 ± 10% with shared control versus 59 ± 23% with human control (p < 0.01). Four participants with transradial amputations also took part in the wider validation; this transfer result should not be read as their result.
details.availability: The paper provides source data and supplementary materials; a public code repository was not identified.

papers.title: Gaze, visual, myoelectric, and inertial data of grasps for intelligent prosthetics
papers.notes: The MeganePro dataset combines EMG, gaze, first-person video and inertial measurements from 30 participants without limb loss and 15 people with transradial amputations. A useful resource for studying multimodal intent prediction.

details.abstract: Problem: research on intelligent prosthetic grasping needs synchronized information about the user’s muscles, gaze and environment. Proposal: release MeganePro, a multimodal dataset for investigating grasp intent and eye–hand coordination.
details.architecture: Dataset paper: no deep-learning model is proposed. The recording setup combines forearm surface EMG and inertial signals with gaze tracking and first-person video.
details.training: Data were collected from 30 participants without limb loss and 15 participants with transradial amputations performing 10 grasp types. These are dataset participants, not a reported model-training split.
details.loss: Not applicable to a new deep-learning model: this is a dataset paper. The authors do use conventional classifiers for technical validation.
details.metrics: Technical validation includes gaze calibration and grasp classification using linear discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbors, and kernel regularized least squares; these are validation baselines, not a proposed deep-learning model.
details.availability: MeganePro Dataset 1 and the authors’ data-processing scripts are archived in Harvard Dataverse; the NinaPro DB10 overview also lists related MeganePro datasets.

papers.title: Bring Your Own Grasp Generator: Leveraging Robot Grasp Generation for Prosthetic Grasping
papers.notes: A shared-autonomy system combines monocular 3D reconstruction and robotic grasp generation to configure a prosthetic hand during reaching, using the user’s motion to help select a grasp.

details.abstract: Problem: selecting and executing a grasp with a multi-degree-of-freedom prosthetic hand can be slow and difficult. Proposal: use an eye-in-hand camera and shared autonomy to infer possible grasps and select one from the user’s reaching trajectory.
details.architecture: The system first estimates how far each visible point is from the camera. DINOv2 is a pretrained vision Transformer that extracts image features; a DPT (Dense Prediction Transformer) head converts those features into a per-pixel depth map in metric units. That map is converted to a 3D point cloud and reduced to 20,000 points. Contact-GraspNet, a neural network for predicting possible gripper poses from a point cloud, proposes candidate grasps. DPVO (Deep Patch Visual Odometry) tracks image patches across camera frames to estimate how the hand moves as the user approaches. The system selects a candidate based on that approach and maps it to the Hannes prosthetic hand.
details.training: The depth model is fine-tuned on SynV2, a Unity-generated synthetic dataset with randomized objects, camera orientation and lighting. The study tested 10 participants without limb loss and 3 with amputations, using 5 objects and 30 trials per person. Three object models appeared in depth training and two were unknown or dissimilar.
details.loss: The paper describes depth-model fine-tuning using the Depth Anything recipe, but does not explicitly specify the loss or training set size in the reported methods.
details.metrics: On the real depth test set, the DINOv2/SynV2 model achieved δ1 = 0.698 and RMSE = 0.113. In the three amputee participants, grasp success was 0.84 ± 0.12 and average grasp time 17.02 ± 4.75 s; the co-contraction baseline was 0.87 ± 0.19 and 24.36 ± 15.07 s. The baseline conditions differed across participants.
details.availability: Code and project are linked below. A public download for the paper’s SynV2 training set was not identified.

papers.title: TinyMyo: a Tiny Foundation Model for Flexible EMG Signal Processing at the Edge
papers.notes: A 3.6-million-parameter Transformer pretrained using masked reconstruction supports several EMG tasks, including gesture classification and hand kinematics regression, and can run on a low-power microcontroller.

details.abstract: Problem: EMG models often struggle to generalize across users and devices, and large models are hard to deploy on wearables. Proposal: pretrain a compact, reusable EMG foundation model with masked signal reconstruction and adapt it to several downstream tasks.
details.architecture: A 3.6M-parameter Transformer encoder with 8 layers, 192-dimensional embeddings and 3 attention heads processes per-channel signal patches. A lightweight linear decoder is used for pretraining; downstream tasks replace it with task-specific heads.
details.training: Pretraining uses NinaPro DB6 (10 subjects), DB7 (20 participants without limb loss and 2 with transradial amputations), and EMG2Pose (193 participants). Signals are 2 kHz, segmented into 1,000-sample windows with 50% overlap; 50% of patches are masked. AdamW uses batch size 512 and a 50-epoch cosine schedule, with 10 warm-up epochs and peak learning rate 1×10⁻⁴.
details.loss: Pretraining: Smooth L1 reconstruction loss on masked patches plus 0.1 times the loss on visible patches. Gesture classification uses cross-entropy; hand-kinematics regression uses L1.
details.metrics: NinaPro DB5: 89.41 ± 0.16% accuracy and 77.97 ± 0.59% F1, fine-tuned with 200 ms windows. EPN-612: 96.74 ± 0.09% accuracy, fine-tuned with 1,000 ms windows. UCI-EMG: 97.56 ± 0.32% accuracy, trained from scratch with 1,000 ms windows. Reported over five seeds. GAP9 inference: 0.785 s and 44.91 mJ.
details.availability: Code and pretrained models are linked below, together with the public pretraining data sources.

papers.title: Agency-Constrained Shared Autonomy for Prosthetic Grasp Selection: A Reproducible Offline Benchmark for Interactive AI in Assistive Robotics
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.notes: An agency budget limits how far autonomous grasp choices may deviate from inferred user intent. The evaluation uses an offline replay benchmark on MeganePro data, not a deployed clinical system.

details.abstract: Problem: an autonomous prosthetic grasp selector can improve task performance while disagreeing with the user’s inferred intent. Proposal: constrain assistance using an explicit agency budget and evaluate the performance–agency trade-off.
details.architecture: No deep network is proposed. Two per-participant multinomial logistic regressions estimate user and autonomy grasp probabilities from forearm acceleration and gaze/pupil features. SetACSA chooses the autonomy-preferred grasp within an agency-feasible set of 10 grasp classes.
details.training: An offline replay benchmark uses MeganePro DB10 data from five participants without limb loss and four with transradial amputations: 3,814 episodes, including 2,715 static and 1,099 dynamic. Per-participant stratified cross-validation yields out-of-fold predictions. EMG and video are not used by these benchmark decoders.
details.loss: The agency loss index is a disagreement proxy used as a decision constraint, not a neural-network training loss. Fixed-budget experiments use τ = 0.10; an adaptive variant varies τ from 0.05 to 0.20. The paper does not specify the logistic-regression optimization loss explicitly.
details.metrics: Across nine participants, SetACSA achieved accuracy 0.580 ± 0.014, macro-F1 0.577 ± 0.014, and agency loss 0.012 ± 0.001; user-only accuracy was 0.532 ± 0.021. Values are mean ± SEM. These are offline results, not evidence from a deployed prosthesis.
details.availability: The benchmark uses the public MeganePro dataset linked below. A public implementation repository was not identified.
